sections.title: Root rules, memory table, and practice

steps.title: Root rules and roots to know
steps.intro: The rules, plus a roots table: blue cells are must-know, white cells are good to know.

tables.title: Rules
head: Rule
Note
rows: a root is a fractional power
power on top, root index on the bottom: \(\sqrt[4]{3^8}=3^2\)
root of a root: multiply the indexes

tables.title: Exam traps
head: Rule
Example
rows: square root vs cube root: 6th power

tips: Number over a root: divide by the number under the root, keep the root. \(\frac{12}{\sqrt6}=(12\div6)\sqrt6=2\sqrt6\).
Inside a square root: never negative. \(\sqrt{x-3}\) exists only for \(x\ge3\).
Root equations: square both sides, then check in the original equation. Or plug in the choices.
Estimate a root between two perfect squares: \(8<\sqrt{70}<9\).

explanation: Find each cube root: \(\sqrt[3]{27}=3\), \(\sqrt[3]{-1}=-1\) (odd roots of negative numbers exist) and \(\sqrt[3]{0}=0\).
The traps: \(2\) forgets that minus a negative is plus, and \(3\) treats \(\sqrt[3]{-1}\) as if it did not exist.
A \(4\)th root is an even root. Any real number to the \(4\)th power is zero or positive. Therefore, no number to the \(4\)th power gives \(-81\).
So, \(\sqrt[4]{-81}\) has no real value. (Careful: \((-3)^4=81\), not \(-81\).)
The power inside goes on top, the root index on the bottom: \(\sqrt[3]{7^6}=7^{\frac63}=7^2=49\).
The trap is \(343=7^3\): it subtracts \(6-3\) instead of dividing \(6\div3\).
A power of \(\frac14\) is a fourth root: \(256^{\frac14}=\sqrt[4]{256}=4\), because \(4^4=256\).
Or take the square root twice: \(\sqrt{256}=16\) and \(\sqrt{16}=4\).
The traps: \(64\) is \(256\cdot\frac14\) (a power is not a product), and \(16\) is only the square root.
The power inside goes on top, the root index goes on the bottom: \(\sqrt[4]{9^6}=9^{\frac64}=9^{\frac32}\).
Take the root first: \(9^{\frac32}=\left(\sqrt9\right)^3=3^3=27\).
The trap: \(6-4=2\) gives \(9^2=81\). Divide the exponents, don't subtract them.
A square root times itself gives the number under the root: \(\sqrt{23}\cdot\sqrt{23}=\sqrt{23\cdot23}=23\).
Put the product under one root: \(\sqrt{20}\cdot\sqrt{5}=\sqrt{20\cdot5}=\sqrt{100}=10\).
Three copies of a cube root multiply back to the number under it: \(\sqrt[3]{6}\cdot\sqrt[3]{6}\cdot\sqrt[3]{6}=\left(\sqrt[3]{6}\right)^3=6\).
Or put everything under one root: \(\sqrt[3]{6\cdot6\cdot6}=\sqrt[3]{216}=6\), because \(6^3=216\).
Put the quotient under one root: \(\frac{\sqrt{98}}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt{\frac{98}{2}}=\sqrt{49}=7\).
Put the quotient under one root: \(\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt{72}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{72}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}}=\frac16\).
The trap is \(\frac1{36}\): it forgets the root at the end.
Write both roots as powers: \(\sqrt{125}=125^{\frac12}\), and the root index \(1.5\) is the power \(\frac{1}{1.5}=\frac23\).
Power of a power: multiply the exponents. \(\left(125^{\frac12}\right)^{\frac23}=125^{\frac12\cdot\frac23}=125^{\frac13}=\sqrt[3]{125}\).
Bring the \(2\) inside the root by squaring it: \(2\sqrt{13}=\sqrt4\cdot\sqrt{13}=\sqrt{4\cdot13}=\sqrt{52}\).
The traps: \(\sqrt{26}\) forgets to square the \(2\), and \(\sqrt{338}=\sqrt{2\cdot169}\) squares the wrong number.
To go inside a cube root, the \(3\) is cubed: \(3\sqrt[3]{4}=\sqrt[3]{27}\cdot\sqrt[3]{4}=\sqrt[3]{27\cdot4}=\sqrt[3]{108}\).
The trap is \(\sqrt[3]{36}=\sqrt[3]{9\cdot4}\): it squares the \(3\), as for a square root.

steps.stem: Which of the following is the largest?
explanation: All four numbers are positive. Compare their squares (this is the same as bringing each number inside the root).
The largest square is \(28\). Therefore \(2\sqrt7=\sqrt{28}\) is the largest.

steps.stem: Which of the following is the smallest?
explanation: Compare each number with \(3\). \(\sqrt[3]{25}\) is less than \(\sqrt[3]{27}=3\).
\(\sqrt{10}\) is more than \(\sqrt9=3\). And \(\pi\) is more than \(3\).
Only \(\sqrt[3]{25}\) is less than \(3\), so it is the smallest. Choice 2.

steps.stem: Which of the following is closest to \(\sqrt{5}\)?
explanation: Square the choices: \(2.2^2=4.84\) and \(2.3^2=5.29\). \(5\) is between them, so \(\sqrt5\) is between \(2.2\) and \(2.3\). Choices 1 and 4 are out.
Which one is closer? The middle between \(2.2\) and \(2.3\) is \(2.25\), and \(2.25^2=5.0625>5\). Therefore, \(\sqrt5<2.25\), closer to \(2.2\).
Plug in the choices. \(x=-2\): \(\sqrt{-2+6}=\sqrt4=2\ne-2\). Not a solution.
\(x=3\): \(\sqrt{3+6}=\sqrt9=3\). A solution.
\(x=6\): \(\sqrt{12}\ne6\). Not a solution. Choice 3 includes \(-2\), which is not a solution.

Why is \(-2\) a trap? After squaring we get \(x+6=x^2\), and \(-2\) solves that: \((-2)^2=4=-2+6\). But a square root is never negative. Therefore, \(\sqrt{x+6}=-2\) is impossible. Only \(x=3\) works.

steps.stem: How many solutions does the equation \(\sqrt{7x}=x\) have?
explanation: Square both sides: \(7x=x^2\). Do not divide by \(x\) (\(x\) can be \(0\)). Move everything to one side and factor: \(x^2-7x=0\), \(x(x-7)=0\).
Therefore \(x=0\) or \(x=7\).
Check both in the original equation: \(\sqrt0=0\) and \(\sqrt{49}=7\). Both work. Therefore, there are \(2\) solutions.
The trap is \(1\): dividing by \(x\) loses the solution \(x=0\).

steps.stem:
Given: \(0<x<1\)
Which of the following is the largest?
explanation: Plug in an easy number between \(0\) and \(1\): \(x=\frac14\).
\(x^2=\frac1{16}\), \(x=\frac14\), \(\sqrt x=\frac12\), \(x^3=\frac1{64}\). The largest is \(\sqrt x=\frac12\).
The rule: for \(0<x<1\), \(x^3<x^2<x<\sqrt x\).

steps.stem: Which of the following is the largest?
explanation: The roots have indexes \(2\), \(3\) and \(6\). Raise every number to the \(6\)th power.
The largest is \(28\). Therefore \(\sqrt[6]{28}\) is the largest.
Multiply the top and the bottom by the partner \(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\).
The bottom: \(\left(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\right)\left(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)=3-2=1\). The top: \(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\).
Therefore \(\frac{1}{\sqrt3-\sqrt2}=\frac{\sqrt3+\sqrt2}{1}=\sqrt3+\sqrt2\).
Check from the answers: \(\left(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\right)\left(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\right)=1\). Therefore, \(\sqrt3+\sqrt2\) is exactly \(1\) divided by \(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\).
The trap: \(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\) is not \(\sqrt1\). Roots do not split over a minus.

steps.stem: What are all the values of \(x\) for which \(\sqrt{2-x}\) is defined?
explanation: The number inside a square root cannot be negative: \(2-x\ge0\).
Therefore \(x\le2\). (\(x=2\) is allowed: \(\sqrt0=0\).)
Split the root: \(\sqrt{9x^2}=\sqrt9\cdot\sqrt{x^2}=3|x|\).
For \(x<0\), \(|x|=-x\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{9x^2}=-3x\).
Example: \(x=-2\). \(\sqrt{9\cdot4}=\sqrt{36}=6\), and \(-3x=-3\cdot(-2)=6\). The trap \(3x\) gives \(-6\): a root is never negative.
Pull out the largest square: \(45=9\cdot5\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{45}=\sqrt{9}\cdot\sqrt5=3\sqrt5\).
Take out the square factors: \(\sqrt{54}=\sqrt{9\cdot6}=3\sqrt{6}\) and \(\sqrt{24}=\sqrt{4\cdot6}=2\sqrt{6}\).
Add like roots: \(3\sqrt{6}+2\sqrt{6}=5\sqrt{6}\).
The trap \(\sqrt{78}\) adds under the root, but \(\sqrt{54}+\sqrt{24}\ne\sqrt{54+24}\).
A power of a power: multiply the exponents. \(3\cdot\frac{2}{3}=2\).

steps.stem: Which of the following is true?
explanation: \(0.5\) is between \(0\) and \(1\). Squaring makes it smaller, and a root makes it bigger.
Difference of squares: \((\sqrt a+\sqrt b)(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)=a-b\).
Therefore \((\sqrt7+\sqrt5)(\sqrt7-\sqrt5)=7-5=2\).
The trap is \(6\): it forgets the middle term \(2\sqrt5\).
Multiply the top and the bottom by the partner \(\sqrt5+1\).
The bottom: \((\sqrt5-1)(\sqrt5+1)=5-1=4\). The top: \(4(\sqrt5+1)\).
Therefore \(\frac{4(\sqrt5+1)}{4}=\sqrt5+1\).
Check from the answers: \((\sqrt5+1)(\sqrt5-1)=4\). Correct.

steps.stem: Which of the following is the smallest?
explanation: The indexes are \(2\), \(3\) and \(6\). Raise every number to the \(6\)th power.
The smallest is \(8\). Therefore \(\sqrt2\) is the smallest.

steps.stem: Which of the following is true?
explanation: Both sides are positive. Compare their squares.
Subtract \(12\) from both: \(2\sqrt{35}\) against \(23\). Bring the \(2\) inside: \(\sqrt{140}\) against \(\sqrt{529}\).
\(\sqrt{140}<\sqrt{529}\). Therefore \(\sqrt5+\sqrt7<\sqrt{35}\).
Choice 4 is the trap: a root does not split over a plus.
